public_rationale: Google's October 26, 2026 FAQ says reviewers assess a subset of nonpublic Gemini chats and that their suggestions help improve its models [e1]. A policy study published October 15, 2025 identifies Google as using chat inputs for training by default, with an opt-out [e2]. Together, these records support the forecast under the contract's reading of use without affirmative opt-in [e1, e2]. Google's August 13, 2025 disclosure provides training exclusions through settings and Temporary Chats, so the evidence does not establish unavoidable use for everyone or disregard of an exercised opt-out [e3].
limitations: The assessment treats default participation as sufficient; it does not establish that Google ignored an exercised opt-out [e1, e2, e3].
The policy study examines disclosed practices rather than underlying training datasets [e2].
Google's disclosed exclusions limit any claim that everyone's private information must be used [e3].

public_payload.normalized_proposition: People's private data will be used to feed data-hungry AI systems, whether or not they like it.

statement.excerpt: Your private data are going to feed the insatiable beast, too — like it or not.

from_speaker: The paradigm we have right now
our_interpretation: The ordinary reading is that AI developers will use people's nonpublic information for training without requiring affirmative permission from each affected person.
Private data includes nonpublic chatbot conversations and uploaded personal material. Public social-media posts alone do not establish this claim.
Default training with an opt-out qualifies as use without affirmative opt-in. It does not establish that a company ignored an exercised opt-out.
The statement predicts a general practice, rather than claiming that every person's private information will inevitably be used.
The phrase 'like it or not' describes how data will be used; it is not a separate conditional antecedent.
criteria.support_condition: A dated disclosure or reliable investigation after publication establishes that a major AI developer uses nonpublic user information for model training without requiring affirmative opt-in permission.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Decisive evidence establishes that the predicted practice cannot occur under the described AI paradigm. An individual company's opt-out or exclusion policy limits the claim's breadth but cannot disprove this open-ended forecast.

evidence.locator: Privacy questions, 'Who has access to my chats, and how does human review improve Gemini for everyone?'
evidence.explanation: Google describes reviewers assessing users' nonpublic conversations and supplying improvements used by its models. The same FAQ explicitly includes generative-model training among uses of saved activity when Keep Activity is enabled; e2 establishes the default-participation policy.

evidence.locator: Table 1 and its explanatory caption, page 1470
evidence.publisher: Proceedings of the AAAI/ACM Conference on AI, Ethics, and Society
evidence.explanation: Table 1 records both default training on chat inputs and an opt-out mechanism for Google. This independent policy analysis corroborates that training participation does not require an affirmative opt-in, although it does not inspect individual training datasets.

evidence.locator: Section 'Control your data with new settings'
evidence.explanation: Google provides an opt-out and temporary conversations excluded from training. This limits any interpretation that every user's information must be used or that an exercised objection is necessarily ignored.

conclusive_event.meets_rule: The FAQ documents actual model improvement using reviewers' suggestions based on nonpublic chats. Combined with e2's evidence of default training participation, this meets the rule requiring a post-publication record of actual use of nonpublic information for model improvement or training under a default-participation policy.
